slide.title: Likely Is Not True
slide.body: Chat bubble reading 'The sun rises in the …' with 'east' highlighted as the next word; beside it, a book icon with a question mark. Small tag: AI Fundamentals · Lesson 9.

scenes.voiceover: A chatbot writes a birthday poem in seconds. Ask it for the source of a quotation, and it may give a book that does not exist, in the same confident voice. How can one system be so helpful, and so wrong?

Welcome to the final week. In the first lesson, you saw generative AI as the smallest circle. It means systems that create new content, such as text, images or sound, instead of only choosing a label, like spam.

slide.title: Predict the next word
slide.body: Text strip: 'The sun rises in the ___'. Below, three candidate words with bars: east (tall), morning (short), sea (very short).

scenes.voiceover: A chatbot is built on a language model. During training, the model reads a very large amount of text. Its job is simple. Look at the words so far, and predict the next word. After the sun rises in the, the word east is very likely.

slide.title: One word at a time
slide.body: An answer builds word by word, each new word sliding in from the right, with a small arrow looping back: predict → add → predict again.

scenes.voiceover: Each time it guesses badly, its dials, the weights from lesson seven, are nudged a little. This repeats over a huge amount of text. Then, when you use the chatbot, it predicts a likely next word, adds it to the answer, and predicts the next one, until the answer is complete.

slide.title: One idea, two results
slide.body: Left, green: Fluency, answers sound natural. Right, orange: Hallucination, sounds correct but is false or invented.

scenes.voiceover: This one idea explains two things. First, fluency. The model has seen so much text that its answers follow the patterns of good writing, so they sound natural. Second, hallucination. That is an answer that sounds correct, but is false or invented.

scenes.on_screen_text: Likely is not the same as true
scenes.voiceover: Why does it happen? The model is trained to produce text that is likely, not text that is true. And it has no built-in sense of I do not know.

scenes.stock_query: confident speaker giving lecture to students
scenes.voiceover: Imagine a person who has listened to many university lectures, but never checked any facts. Ask them a question, and they answer like a professor, with the right words and the right confidence. Sometimes they are right. Sometimes they fill a gap with something that only sounds right. From their voice alone, you cannot tell which.

slide.title: Images too
slide.body: Text prompt box → 'learned patterns from images + descriptions' → a new illustrated picture. Small inset: a drawn hand with six fingers circled.

scenes.voiceover: Image generators work in a similar way. They learn patterns from many images and their descriptions, then build a new image that fits your words. They do not copy one stored picture. And they also make errors, like a hand with the wrong number of fingers.

scenes.stock_query: teacher planning lesson on laptop at desk
scenes.voiceover: Let's see both results in one task. Rafael is a secondary school history teacher in Porto, Portugal. He uses a chatbot to prepare a lesson about ocean trade routes.

slide.title: Task 1: an introduction
slide.body: Generic chat mock-up. Request: 'Write a short, simple introduction to trade routes for 13-year-olds.' Answer: a tidy paragraph. Green tick: fluent, easy to check.

scenes.voiceover: First, he asks it to write a short, simple introduction to trade routes for thirteen year olds. The result is clear and well organised. This task needs fluent, general writing, and Rafael can check it just by reading.

slide.title: Task 2: a reading list
slide.body: Generic chat mock-up. Request for three books with authors and page numbers. Answer: three neatly formatted entries with invented titles, authors and page numbers.

scenes.voiceover: Next, he asks for three books about Portuguese sea trade, with authors and page numbers for key quotations. The chatbot gives three titles, three authors and exact page numbers. It looks perfect.

slide.title: Rafael checks
slide.body: Book 1: real (green tick) · Book 2: real author, title does not exist (orange) · Book 3: cannot be found (red cross)

scenes.voiceover: Rafael checks his school library catalogue and an online bookshop. One book is real. One real author is listed with a book title that does not exist. And the third book cannot be found anywhere.

Why? A list of books with authors and page numbers is a common shape of text. The model produced that shape, without checking that each item was real. So Rafael keeps the introduction, removes the reading list, and builds his own list from the library catalogue.

slide.title: A confident tone is not evidence
slide.body: Treat any fact, number, name or source from a chatbot as a claim to check.

scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to think that a chatbot is a smarter search engine. It generates text from patterns. Some chatbots can also search the web, but the final answer is still generated. A confident tone is not evidence. Treat any fact, number, name or source as a claim to check.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Language models predict the next word, one word at a time 2. Likely ≠ true: fluency and hallucination 3. Draft and explain with chatbots; verify facts, names, numbers, sources

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a language model is trained to predict the next word, and a chatbot builds its answer one predicted word at a time. Second, this explains both fluency and hallucination. The model produces text that is likely, which is not always true. Third, use chatbots for drafting and explaining, and always check facts, names, numbers and sources.

scenes.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, ask ChatGPT or Claude three factual questions that you can check. Verify each answer in a reliable source, and record any errors. In the next lesson, we look at where AI goes wrong for whole groups of people, in Bias, Data and the Limits of AI. See you there.
